title: Offboarding Security for Small Companies
summary: When someone leaves a small company, nobody knows which of 50 tools they can still access. Find and remove it all in one click.
hook: "He left 4 months ago. Why is his account still logged into our AWS and our customer database?"
story:
**A 35-person marketing agency uses about 50 cloud tools:** Google Workspace, Slack, Figma, Notion, HubSpot, AWS, Canva, a password manager and many more. When a designer leaves, the office manager disables her Google account and assumes that's enough.

But she signed up to **12 tools with her own password**, shared files publicly, and still has access to a client's ad account. Nobody has a list. Months later, a former employee's old account is used to **log in and download client data**.

whyReal.title: Every company has people leaving
whyReal.text: Staff turnover happens all the time, and each departure is a security moment.

whyReal.title: Small companies have no IT team
whyReal.text: There's no one whose job is "remove access everywhere".

whyReal.title: Real security and compliance risk
whyReal.text: Former employees with access are a known cause of data leaks, and security questionnaires (idea ①) ask about offboarding.

whyReal.title: But: competitors exist
whyReal.text: SaaS-management tools exist, mostly aimed at mid-size and larger companies with matching prices.

whoPays.label: Customer
whoPays.text: companies with 10–150 employees and no dedicated IT/security person (agencies, startups, consultancies).

whoPays.label: Market
whoPays.text: global, starting with companies on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.

solution.title: Connect
solution.text: one click to connect Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 (admin).

solution.title: Discover
solution.text: we find every app employees signed into with Google/Microsoft, plus licences and shared files.

solution.title: Map
solution.text: each person gets a profile: "Sarah uses 23 apps, admin in 4, owns 312 shared files".

solution.title: Offboard
solution.text: when someone leaves, click "Offboard Sarah" to get a checklist, automatic removal where APIs allow, and ownership transfer of files.

solution.title: Prove it
solution.text: a report shows everything removed, with timestamps, ready for audits or security questionnaires.

solution.title: Monitor
solution.text: weekly alerts for risky things like public file links or ex-employees still active.

later: Auto-removal in Slack, GitHub, Notion, AWS…
Link with idea ① (security questionnaire answers)

techStack: Google Workspace Admin SDK / Microsoft Graph
strong security practices (encryption, least privilege) since we hold admin access

timeline.what: **Validate.** Ask 15 small companies: "What happens when someone leaves?" Do a free manual audit for 3 of them.
Google Workspace connection, app discovery, access view.
Offboarding flow, reports, first paying customers.

questions: When someone left recently, what exactly did you do to remove their access?
How many tools does your team use? Do you have a list?
Who is responsible for IT and security at your company?
Have you ever found an ex-employee still had access somewhere?
Do customers ask about your offboarding process in security questionnaires?
